Translation 'the Fear of Yitzchaq' follows the ASV/traditional objective-genitive reading (Alt 1929, Westermann p. 498, Speiser AB). Narrative-functional reading (ethno-linguistic pivot) is mainstream.
*Ha-gal ha-zeh ed beini u-veinekha* — etymology made explicit.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁמַ֗ע אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֤י בְנֵֽי־לָבָן֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר לָקַ֣ח יַעֲקֹ֔ב אֵ֖ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְאָבִ֑ינוּ וּמֵאֲשֶׁ֣ר לְאָבִ֔ינוּ עָשָׂ֕ה אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַכָּבֹ֖ד הַזֶּֽה׃

i18n.en: And he heard the words of Lavan's sons, saying, Ya'aqov has taken away all that was our father's; and of that which was our father's has he gotten all this wealth.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֥רְא יַעֲקֹ֖ב אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י לָבָ֑ן וְהִנֵּ֥ה אֵינֶ֛נּוּ עִמּ֖וֹ כִּתְמ֥וֹל שִׁלְשֽׁוֹם׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov saw the face of Lavan, and behold, it was not toward him as yesterday and the day before.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶֽל־יַעֲקֹ֔ב שׁ֛וּב אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ אֲבוֹתֶ֖יךָ וּלְמוֹלַדְתֶּ֑ךָ וְאֶֽהְיֶ֖ה עִמָּֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And YHWH said to Ya'aqov, Return to the land of your fathers, and to your kindred; and I will be with you.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח יַעֲקֹ֔ב וַיִּקְרָ֖א לְרָחֵ֣ל וּלְלֵאָ֑ה הַשָּׂדֶ֖ה אֶל־צֹאנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov sent and called Rachel and Le'ah to the field unto his flock,

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֗ן רֹאֶ֤ה אָנֹכִי֙ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י אֲבִיכֶ֔ן כִּֽי־אֵינֶ֥נּוּ אֵלַ֖י כִּתְמֹ֣ל שִׁלְשֹׁ֑ם וֵֽאלֹהֵ֣י אָבִ֔י הָיָ֖ה עִמָּדִֽי׃

i18n.en: and said to them, I see your father's face, that it is not toward me as yesterday and the day before; but the Elohim of my father has been with me.

paragraphs.text: וְאַתֵּ֖נָה יְדַעְתֶּ֑ן כִּ֚י בְּכָל־כֹּחִ֔י עָבַ֖דְתִּי אֶת־אֲבִיכֶֽן׃

i18n.en: And you yourselves know that with all my strength I have served your father.

paragraphs.text: וַאֲבִיכֶן֙ הֵ֣תֶל בִּ֔י וְהֶחֱלִ֥ף אֶת־מַשְׂכֻּרְתִּ֖י עֲשֶׂ֣רֶת מֹנִ֑ים וְלֹֽא־נְתָנ֣וֹ אֱלֹהִ֔ים לְהָרַ֖ע עִמָּדִֽי׃

i18n.en: And your father has deceived me, and changed my wages ten times; but Elohim did not allow him to harm me.

paragraphs.text: אִם־כֹּ֣ה יֹאמַ֗ר נְקֻדִּים֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה שְׂכָרֶ֔ךָ וְיָלְד֥וּ כָל־הַצֹּ֖אן נְקֻדִּ֑ים וְאִם־כֹּ֣ה יֹאמַ֗ר עֲקֻדִּים֙ יִהְיֶ֣ה שְׂכָרֶ֔ךָ וְיָלְד֥וּ כָל־הַצֹּ֖אן עֲקֻדִּֽים׃

i18n.en: If he said thus, The speckled shall be your wages, then all the flock bore speckled; and if he said thus, The streaked shall be your wages, then all the flock bore streaked.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּצֵּ֧ל אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־מִקְנֵ֥ה אֲבִיכֶ֖ם וַיִּתֶּן־לִֽי׃

i18n.en: Thus Elohim has taken away the livestock of your father, and given them to me.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י בְּעֵת֙ יַחֵ֣ם הַצֹּ֔אן וָאֶשָּׂ֥א עֵינַ֛י וָאֵ֖רֶא בַּחֲל֑וֹם וְהִנֵּ֤ה הָֽעַתֻּדִים֙ הָעֹלִ֣ים עַל־הַצֹּ֔אן עֲקֻדִּ֥ים נְקֻדִּ֖ים וּבְרֻדִּֽים׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass at the time that the flock conceived, that I lifted up my eyes, and saw in a dream, and behold, the he-goats which leaped upon the flock were streaked, speckled, and grizzled.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלַ֜י מַלְאַ֧ךְ הָאֱלֹהִ֛ים בַּחֲל֖וֹם יַֽעֲקֹ֑ב וָאֹמַ֖ר הִנֵּֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And the messenger of the Elohim said to me in the dream, Ya'aqov; and I said, Here am I.

notes.official:
**The verse uses *mal'akh ha-Elohim* — *the messenger of the Elohim* — with the definite article and with *ha-Elohim* (the deity-class designation) rather than *YHWH*.** מַלְאַךְ הָאֱלֹהִים. The construction is grammatically and registrally distinct from *mal'akh YHWH*, and falls under the [malakh-elohim-messenger](#malakh-elohim-messenger) entry (whose anchor was Gen 21:17 — the second Hagar-scene — and which v2.29.0 expands to include this verse).

**The internal cross-reference at v 13 is decisive.** The same messenger continues speaking at v 12 and at v 13 identifies himself as *ha-El Beit-El* — *the El of Beit-El* — recalling the Gen 28 Bethel theophany (the matzevah-anointing, the vow). The messenger's self-identification with the Bethel-deity makes the v 11 *mal'akh ha-Elohim* the same figure who appeared to Ya'aqov in the Bethel ladder-vision (Gen 28:12, *mal'akhei Elohim olim v-yoredim bo*). The source-critical reading attributes both the Gen 28 ladder-scene and the Gen 31 dream to the E-document, with the *Elohim* / *ha-Elohim* divine-name register and the *mal'akh*-mediated mode of revelation consistent across the two passages (Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 491-493; Speiser AB *Genesis* 1964 pp. 245-246).

**Editorial correction note (v2.29.0).** Prior glossary releases had erroneously listed GEN-31:11 under the `malakh-yhwh-messenger` *appliesTo* array. The verse uses *ha-Elohim*, not *YHWH*, and properly belongs under `malakh-elohim-messenger`. The v2.29.0 release removes GEN-WOH-31:11 / GEN-31:11 from the *malakh-yhwh-messenger* anchor-list and adds it to *malakh-elohim-messenger*. The translation renders *the messenger of the Elohim* (preserving the article and the *Elohim* lexeme), matching the chapter's wider *ha-Elohim*-register.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר שָׂא־נָ֨א עֵינֶ֤יךָ וּרְאֵה֙ כָּל־הָֽעַתֻּדִים֙ הָעֹלִ֣ים עַל־הַצֹּ֔אן עֲקֻדִּ֥ים נְקֻדִּ֖ים וּבְרֻדִּ֑ים כִּ֣י רָאִ֔יתִי אֵ֛ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר לָבָ֖ן עֹ֥שֶׂה לָּֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And he said, Lift up now your eyes, and see: all the he-goats which leap upon the flock are streaked, speckled, and grizzled; for I have seen all that Lavan does to you.

paragraphs.text: אָנֹכִ֤י הָאֵל֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר מָשַׁ֤חְתָּ שָּׁם֙ מַצֵּבָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר נָדַ֥רְתָּ לִּ֛י שָׁ֖ם נֶ֑דֶר עַתָּ֗ה ק֥וּם צֵא֙ מִן־הָאָ֣רֶץ הַזֹּ֔את וְשׁ֖וּב אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ מוֹלַדְתֶּֽךָ׃

i18n.en: I am the El of Beit-El, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me; now arise, get out of this land, and return to the land of your kindred.

notes.official:
***Anokhi ha-El Beit-El* — *I am the El of Beit-El* — is one of the Hebrew Bible's few divine self-identifications with a place-name.** אָנֹכִי הָאֵל בֵּית־אֵל. The construction names the deity by the cult-site at which he is locally encountered, with the definite article (*ha-El*) and the place-name in apposition. The pattern recurs sparsely across Genesis at Gen 16:13 (*El Ro'i*), Gen 21:33 (*YHWH El Olam*), Gen 33:20 (*El Elohei Yisra'el*), and Gen 35:7 (*El Beit-El* — Ya'aqov's altar-name on the return-from-Padan-Aram); the Gen 31:13 instance is the deity's *own* self-disclosure, where the others are human-given names.

**The construction belongs to the patriarchal El-of-the-fathers religion** as reconstructed by **Alt** (*Der Gott der Väter* 1929) and developed by **Cross** (*Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic* 1973, ch. 1). The El-compound divine-naming pattern — *El Elyon*, *El Ro'i*, *El Shaddai*, *El Olam*, *El Beit-El*, *El Elohei Yisra'el* — encodes a pre-Israelite West-Semitic local-sanctuary El-cult subsequently harmonized with YHWH; each compound localizes the deity at a specific cult-site. The Gen 31:13 self-identification explicitly links the messenger-figure of v 11 to the Bethel-theophany of Gen 28: the *matzevah* anointed at Gen 28:18 and the vow at Gen 28:20-22 are recalled in the same verse, marking the present dream-revelation as the same divine encounter resumed across the Padan-Aram interval.

The ASV-baseline *the God of Bethel* collapses *El* into the generic and obscures the patriarchal-El-cult signal. The WoH translation preserves *the El of Beit-El* — *El* in transliteration, the place-name in apposition — matching the project's practice with the other El-compounds. The cross-link to the Bethel-vow material (the [matzevah-sacred-pillar-patriarchal-religion](#matzevah-sacred-pillar-patriarchal-religion) entry) is preserved through the *matzevah* recall.

paragraphs.text: וַתַּ֤עַן רָחֵל֙ וְלֵאָ֔ה וַתֹּאמַ֖רְנָה ל֑וֹ הַע֥וֹד לָ֛נוּ חֵ֥לֶק וְנַחֲלָ֖ה בְּבֵ֥ית אָבִֽינוּ׃

i18n.en: And Rachel and Le'ah answered and said to him, Is there yet any portion or inheritance for us in our father's house?

paragraphs.text: הֲל֧וֹא נָכְרִיּ֛וֹת נֶחְשַׁ֥בְנוּ ל֖וֹ כִּ֣י מְכָרָ֑נוּ וַיֹּ֥אכַל גַּם־אָכ֖וֹל אֶת־כַּסְפֵּֽנוּ׃

i18n.en: Are we not accounted by him as foreigners? For he has sold us, and has also entirely consumed our money.

paragraphs.text: כִּ֣י כָל־הָעֹ֗שֶׁר אֲשֶׁ֨ר הִצִּ֤יל אֱלֹהִים֙ מֵֽאָבִ֔ינוּ לָ֥נוּ ה֖וּא וּלְבָנֵ֑ינוּ וְעַתָּ֗ה כֹּל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָמַ֧ר אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֵלֶ֖יךָ עֲשֵֽׂה׃

i18n.en: For all the riches which Elohim has taken away from our father, that is ours and our children's; now then, whatever Elohim has said to you, do.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֖קָם יַעֲקֹ֑ב וַיִּשָּׂ֛א אֶת־בָּנָ֥יו וְאֶת־נָשָׁ֖יו עַל־הַגְּמַלִּֽים׃

i18n.en: Then Ya'aqov rose up, and set his sons and his wives upon the camels;

paragraphs.text: וַיִּנְהַ֣ג אֶת־כָּל־מִקְנֵ֗הוּ וְאֶת־כָּל־רְכֻשׁוֹ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר רָכָ֔שׁ מִקְנֵה֙ קִנְיָנ֔וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר רָכַ֖שׁ בְּפַדַּ֣ן אֲרָ֑ם לָב֛וֹא אֶל־יִצְחָ֥ק אָבִ֖יו אַ֥רְצָה כְּנָֽעַן׃

i18n.en: and he drove away all his livestock, and all his property which he had gathered, the livestock of his acquiring, which he had gathered in Padan-Aram, to go to Yitzchaq his father, to the land of Kena'an.

paragraphs.text: וְלָבָ֣ן הָלַ֔ךְ לִגְזֹ֖ז אֶת־צֹאנ֑וֹ וַתִּגְנֹ֣ב רָחֵ֔ל אֶת־הַתְּרָפִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְאָבִֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: Now Lavan had gone to shear his sheep; and Rachel stole the teraphim that were her father's.

notes.official:
**The *teraphim* (תְּרָפִים) are one of the Hebrew Bible's most editorially-load-bearing cultic-material-culture nouns** — a class of household-cultic-objects (figurines, statues, cult-images) of disputed form and function whose attestations span the patriarchal narratives through the post-exilic prophets. *Va-tignov Rachel et-ha-teraphim asher l-aviha* — *Rachel stole the teraphim that were her father's*. The lexeme is preserved in transliteration (matching the WoH practice with *matzevah*, *eshel*, *Elohim*) over the ASV/KJV *images*, the NRSV/NJPS *household gods*, and the NIV *family idols* — each of which preempts the cultic-object's contested form, function, or polemical-register.

**The cross-corpus distribution is concentrated and editorially load-bearing.** Patriarchal: Gen 31:19, 31:34-35 (here). The Mikhah-Danite priesthood cycle: **Judg 17:5**, **Judg 18:14-20** (the *pesel u-massekhah ephod u-teraphim* — *the carved image and molten image, ephod and teraphim* — as a fixed household-shrine inventory). The David-and-Mikhal scene: **1 Sam 19:13-16** (Mikhal substitutes a *teraphim* under the blanket for David in the bed — implying an anthropomorphic, life-size form). The Deuteronomistic-polemical: **1 Sam 15:23** (*aven u-teraphim* — *iniquity and teraphim* — Samuel's indictment of Saul); **2 Kgs 23:24** (Josiah's reform removes the teraphim). The prophetic: **Hos 3:4** (Israel without *zevach u-matzevah ... ephod u-teraphim* — the standard inventory); **Ezek 21:26 [MT 21:21]** (Nebuchadnezzar at the road-fork consulting teraphim, casting lots, and inspecting the liver — three divinatory methods juxtaposed); **Zech 10:2** (*ha-teraphim diberu aven* — *the teraphim speak vanity*).

**The function is plurally attested:** divinatory consultation (Ezek 21:26; Zech 10:2); household-protection and ancestor-cult (the Genesis-31 / Nuzi-parallel reading); anthropomorphic cult-image (1 Sam 19:13-16). The lexeme's etymology is contested — Hoffner *JBL* 86 (1967) derives from Hittite *tarpis* (*demon, spirit*); alternative derivations from *raphah* (*be slack*) or *taraph* (*enjoy life*) — and the form-disputed question (figurines vs. life-size statues) is reconcilable if the lexeme covers a class of cult-objects of varying size and function rather than a single type.

**The Nuzi-parallel reading is editorially significant for Rachel's theft.** The Nuzi cuneiform tablets (15th-century Hurrian texts from the Mitanni-period Tell el-Faḫḫar near Kirkuk) attest household-gods (*ilānū*) as legal-inheritance-tokens: possession of the household-gods marks the primary-heir status in patrimonial-inheritance disputes. **Speiser** AB *Genesis* 1964 pp. 250-251 reads Rachel's theft as a legal-inheritance-claim deployment of the Nuzi-parallel — Rachel is securing inheritance-status against her father's sons (cf. her and Le'ah's complaint at vv 14-16 about being *accounted as foreigners* and disinherited). The reading has been contested in subsequent ANE-comparative scholarship (Greenberg *JBL* 81, 1962, *Another Look at Rachel's Theft of the Teraphim* — disputes the legal-token reading; van der Toorn *VT* 40, 1990, *The Nature of the Biblical Teraphim in the Light of the Cuneiform Evidence* — preserves a modified version, reading the teraphim as ancestor-cult-statues whose possession carried both religious and legal weight) but remains the standard background for the Genesis-31 interpretation.

**Modern critical synthesis.** Van der Toorn 1990 reads the teraphim as household ancestor-cult-statues whose possession carried inheritance-legal weight. Albertz *A History of Israelite Religion* 1994 vol. 1 reads them within the household-shrine religion stratum. Smith *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism* 2001 reads them as part of the family-religion layer beneath the official-Yahwistic cult. Rachel's theft thus carries both religious dimensions (the cult-objects of her father's house) and legal dimensions (the inheritance-token reading). The chapter's narrative-irony — Rachel hides the cult-objects under a menstrual-impurity pretext at v 35 — depends on both readings: the teraphim are sacred enough that their concealment is significant, and weighty enough that Lavan's search is the legal-pursuit of a stolen-inheritance-token. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 218-220; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 493-495; Hamilton *NICOT* 1995 pp. 302-303; Wenham *WBC* 1994 pp. 273-275.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגְנֹ֣ב יַעֲקֹ֔ב אֶת־לֵ֥ב לָבָ֖ן הָאֲרַמִּ֑י עַל־בְּלִי֙ הִגִּ֣יד ל֔וֹ כִּ֥י בֹרֵ֖חַ הֽוּא׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov stole away unawares to Lavan the Arami, in that he did not tell him that he was fleeing.

notes.official:
***Va-yignov Ya'aqov et-lev Lavan ha-Arami* — *Ya'aqov stole the heart of Lavan the Arami*.** The construct *ganav et-lev* (*steal the heart*) is a fixed Hebrew idiom for *deceive by stealth, outwit*, recurring at 2 Sam 15:6 (Avshalom *va-yganev Avshalom et-lev anshei Yisra'el* — *Avshalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel*).

**The chapter is built around the *g-n-v* (steal) verbal cluster.** Seven deployments in fifty-four verses: v 19 (Rachel steals the teraphim, literal); v 20 (Ya'aqov steals Lavan's heart, idiomatic); v 26 (Lavan's accusation *va-tignov et-levavi*, idiomatic); v 27 (*va-tignov oti*, idiomatic); v 30 (*lamah ganavta et-elohai*, literal); v 32 (*Rachel genavatam*, literal); v 39 (*genuvti yom u-genuvti lailah*, literal — twice). Four idiomatic deployments cluster around Ya'aqov-and-Lavan's mutual deception; three literal deployments around the teraphim-theft and the flock-theft accusations. The cluster names the chapter's theme: a fugitive-family-flight set in the language-field of *theft* and structured by parallel grievances — Rachel against her father, Ya'aqov against his father-in-law, Lavan against both.

The translation preserves the ASV-baseline *stole away unawares to Lavan* (smoothing the idiom into English) over the literal *stole the heart of Lavan*; the verbal-cluster is documented in the [ganav-et-lev-deceive-idiom](#ganav-et-lev-deceive-idiom) glossary entry.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּבְרַ֥ח הוּא֙ וְכָל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֔וֹ וַיָּ֖קָם וַיַּעֲבֹ֣ר אֶת־הַנָּהָ֑ר וַיָּ֥שֶׂם אֶת־פָּנָ֖יו הַ֥ר הַגִּלְעָֽד׃

i18n.en: So he fled with all that he had; and he rose up, and crossed the River, and set his face toward the mountain of Gil'ad.

paragraphs.text: וַיֻּגַּ֥ד לְלָבָ֖ן בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֑י כִּ֥י בָרַ֖ח יַעֲקֹֽב׃

i18n.en: And it was told Lavan on the third day that Ya'aqov had fled.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֤ח אֶת־אֶחָיו֙ עִמּ֔וֹ וַיִּרְדֹּ֣ף אַחֲרָ֔יו דֶּ֖רֶךְ שִׁבְעַ֣ת יָמִ֑ים וַיַּדְבֵּ֥ק אֹת֖וֹ בְּהַ֥ר הַגִּלְעָֽד׃

i18n.en: And he took his kinsmen with him, and pursued after him a journey of seven days; and he overtook him in the mountain of Gil'ad.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֧א אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶל־לָבָ֥ן הָאֲרַמִּ֖י בַּחֲלֹ֣ם הַלָּ֑יְלָה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ הִשָּׁ֧מֶר לְךָ֛ פֶּן־תְּדַבֵּ֥ר עִֽם־יַעֲקֹ֖ב מִטּ֥וֹב עַד־רָֽע׃

i18n.en: And Elohim came to Lavan the Arami in a dream of the night, and said to him, Take heed to yourself that you speak not to Ya'aqov from good to bad.

notes.official:
**The verse is verbally near-identical to Gen 20:3** — *va-yavo Elohim el-Lavan ha-Arami ba-chalom ha-lailah* echoes *va-yavo Elohim el-Avimelekh ba-chalom ha-lailah* — the Abimelekh dream-warning of Gen 20:3. Both instances stage the same pattern: a non-Israelite man with morally-ambiguous standing toward the patriarchal-family is warned by Elohim in a night-dream not to harm the patriarch. The dream-revelation mode is the canonical HB medium for divine address to non-Israelite figures (Avimelekh; Lavan; Pharaoh at Gen 41; Nebuchadnezzar at Dan 2, 4). See [divine-dream-communication-formula](#divine-dream-communication-formula).

**The *tov-ra* merism.** *Mi-tov ad-ra* — *from good to bad* — is a HB rhetorical-construction naming a totality by its two extremes. The construction recurs at 2 Sam 13:22 (Avshalom and Amnon — *l-me-ra v-ad-tov*, inverted); 2 Sam 14:17 (the Tekoite woman); the Eden-tree's *tov va-ra* (Gen 2:9, 2:17). At Gen 31:24 the merism functions as a comprehensive speech-prohibition: Lavan is barred from *any* significant address to Ya'aqov, from one extreme to the other. The repetition at v 29 in Lavan's own retelling confirms the merism's importance. See [tov-ra-merism](#tov-ra-merism). Sarna p. 219; Honeyman *VT* 2 (1952) on the merism-pattern; Westermann pp. 495-496.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּשֵּׂ֥ג לָבָ֖ן אֶֽת־יַעֲקֹ֑ב וְיַעֲקֹ֗ב תָּקַ֤ע אֶֽת־אָהֳלוֹ֙ בָּהָ֔ר וְלָבָ֛ן תָּקַ֥ע אֶת־אֶחָ֖יו בְּהַ֥ר הַגִּלְעָֽד׃

i18n.en: And Lavan overtook Ya'aqov. Now Ya'aqov had pitched his tent in the mountain; and Lavan with his kinsmen encamped in the mountain of Gil'ad.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָבָן֙ לְיַעֲקֹ֔ב מֶ֣ה עָשִׂ֔יתָ וַתִּגְנֹ֖ב אֶת־לְבָבִ֑י וַתְּנַהֵג֙ אֶת־בְּנֹתַ֔י כִּשְׁבֻי֖וֹת חָֽרֶב׃

i18n.en: And Lavan said to Ya'aqov, What have you done, that you have stolen my heart, and carried away my daughters as captives of the sword?

paragraphs.text: לָ֤מָּה נַחְבֵּ֙אתָ֙ לִבְרֹ֔חַ וַתִּגְנֹ֖ב אֹתִ֑י וְלֹא־הִגַּ֣דְתָּ לִּ֔י וָֽאֲשַׁלֵּחֲךָ֛ בְּשִׂמְחָ֥ה וּבְשִׁרִ֖ים בְּתֹ֥ף וּבְכִנּֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: Why did you flee secretly, and steal away from me, and did not tell me, that I might have sent you away with mirth and with songs, with timbrel and with lyre?

paragraphs.text: וְלֹ֣א נְטַשְׁתַּ֔נִי לְנַשֵּׁ֥ק לְבָנַ֖י וְלִבְנֹתָ֑י עַתָּ֖ה הִסְכַּ֥לְתָּֽ עֲשֽׂוֹ׃

i18n.en: And have not allowed me to kiss my sons and my daughters? Now you have done foolishly.

paragraphs.text: יֶשׁ־לְאֵ֣ל יָדִ֔י לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת עִמָּכֶ֖ם רָ֑ע וֵֽאלֹהֵ֨י אֲבִיכֶ֜ם אֶ֣מֶשׁ ׀ אָמַ֧ר אֵלַ֣י לֵאמֹ֗ר הִשָּׁ֧מֶר לְךָ֛ מִדַּבֵּ֥ר עִֽם־יַעֲקֹ֖ב מִטּ֥וֹב עַד־רָֽע׃

i18n.en: It is in the power of my hand to do you harm; but the Elohim of your father spoke to me last night, saying, Take heed to yourself that you speak not to Ya'aqov from good to bad.

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּה֙ הָלֹ֣ךְ הָלַ֔כְתָּ כִּֽי־נִכְסֹ֥ף נִכְסַ֖פְתָּה לְבֵ֣ית אָבִ֑יךָ לָ֥מָּה גָנַ֖בְתָּ אֶת־אֱלֹהָֽי׃

i18n.en: And now, though you would surely go, because you sorely longed for your father's house, yet why have you stolen my elohim?

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֥עַן יַעֲקֹ֖ב וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְלָבָ֑ן כִּ֣י יָרֵ֔אתִי כִּ֣י אָמַ֔רְתִּי פֶּן־תִּגְזֹ֥ל אֶת־בְּנוֹתֶ֖יךָ מֵעִמִּֽי׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov answered and said to Lavan, Because I was afraid; for I said, Lest you should take your daughters from me by force.

paragraphs.text: עִ֠ם אֲשֶׁ֨ר תִּמְצָ֣א אֶת־אֱלֹהֶיךָ֮ לֹ֣א יִֽחְיֶה֒ נֶ֣גֶד אַחֵ֧ינוּ הַֽכֶּר־לְךָ֛ מָ֥ה עִמָּדִ֖י וְקַֽח־לָ֑ךְ וְלֹֽא־יָדַ֣ע יַעֲקֹ֔ב כִּ֥י רָחֵ֖ל גְּנָבָֽתַם׃

i18n.en: With whomever you find your elohim, he shall not live. Before our kinsmen, identify for yourself what is with me, and take it. For Ya'aqov did not know that Rachel had stolen them.

notes.official:
**Ya'aqov's accidental death-sentence — *im asher timtza et-Eloheka lo yichye* — *with whomever you find your elohim, he shall not live*.** The verse continues *v-lo yada Ya'aqov ki Rachel genavatam* — *and Ya'aqov did not know that Rachel had stolen them*. The narrator's parenthetical aside flags the death-sentence as unwittingly self-fulfilling: Rachel is the one in possession of the teraphim, and Ya'aqov has just pronounced death on whoever holds them.

**Classical and modern commentary read v 32 as the narrative-anticipation of Rachel's death in childbirth at Gen 35:18-20** — the death-of-Rachel notice on the way to Efrat, the *ben-oni* / *Binyamin* renaming, the pillar at her burial-site. The narrative-anticipation reading is foundational in rabbinic tradition (Genesis Rabbah 74:9; Rashi at Gen 31:32 — *me-elalat Ya'aqov metah Rachel ba-derekh* — *because of Ya'aqov's curse Rachel died on the way*) and is widely held in modern critical commentary (Sarna *JPS* 1989 pp. 219; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 p. 496; Wenham *WBC* 1994 p. 277). The chapter's irony is layered: Ya'aqov's confident pronouncement of innocence-by-search becomes a curse on his beloved wife; Rachel's clever concealment at v 35 saves her in the immediate scene but does not avert the longer-term consequence.

**The lexeme *Eloheka* (*your elohim*).** Lavan's terminology for the teraphim at v 30 (*lamah ganavta et-elohai* — *why have you stolen my elohim*) is taken up by Ya'aqov at v 32 (*timtza et-Eloheka* — *you find your elohim*). The narrative-incidental usage marks the teraphim as belonging to the *elohim*-category — *elohim* as a class-noun for cult-objects or lesser deities rather than as the supreme deity. The same category-usage recurs at Exod 22:8-9 (the judges as *elohim*); Ps 82:1, 6 (the divine council as *elohim*); and in the wider patriarchal-period stratum where *elohim* names a category of divine-or-semi-divine beings. The WoH translation preserves the lowercase plural-form *elohim* throughout the chapter, matching the project's practice with *elohim*-as-category at Gen 6:2-4 and the cross-corpus loci.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֨א לָבָ֜ן בְּאֹ֥הֶל יַעֲקֹ֣ב ׀ וּבְאֹ֣הֶל לֵאָ֗ה וּבְאֹ֛הֶל שְׁתֵּ֥י הָאֲמָהֹ֖ת וְלֹ֣א מָצָ֑א וַיֵּצֵא֙ מֵאֹ֣הֶל לֵאָ֔ה וַיָּבֹ֖א בְּאֹ֥הֶל רָחֵֽל׃

i18n.en: And Lavan went into Ya'aqov's tent, and into Le'ah's tent, and into the tent of the two handmaids; but he did not find them. And he came out of Le'ah's tent, and entered into Rachel's tent.

paragraphs.text: וְרָחֵ֞ל לָקְחָ֣ה אֶת־הַתְּרָפִ֗ים וַתְּשִׂמֵ֛ם בְּכַ֥ר הַגָּמָ֖ל וַתֵּ֣שֶׁב עֲלֵיהֶ֑ם וַיְמַשֵּׁ֥שׁ לָבָ֛ן אֶת־כָּל־הָאֹ֖הֶל וְלֹ֥א מָצָֽא׃

i18n.en: Now Rachel had taken the teraphim, and put them in the camel's saddle, and sat upon them. And Lavan felt about all the tent, but did not find them.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל־אָבִ֗יהָ אַל־יִ֙חַר֙ בְּעֵינֵ֣י אֲדֹנִ֔י כִּ֣י ל֤וֹא אוּכַל֙ לָק֣וּם מִפָּנֶ֔יךָ כִּי־דֶ֥רֶךְ נָשִׁ֖ים לִ֑י וַיְחַפֵּ֕שׂ וְלֹ֥א מָצָ֖א אֶת־הַתְּרָפִֽים׃

i18n.en: And she said to her father, Let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before you; for the way of women is upon me. And he searched, but did not find the teraphim.

notes.official:
***Ki derekh nashim li* — *for the way of women is upon me*.** The construct *derekh nashim* (*the way of women*) is the Hebrew Bible's standard euphemism for menstruation. The same euphemism recurs idiomatically at Gen 18:11 (Sarah's *chadal lihyot l-Sarah orach k-nashim* — *the way after the manner of women had ceased to be with Sarah*); the related *niddah* terminology of Lev 15:19-30, 18:19, 20:18 codifies the ritual-purity legislation. The lexeme *derekh* here carries the *manner / condition* sense rather than the *path / road* sense.

**Rachel's claim is a double-function speech-act.** First, it explains her not rising in her father's presence — a courtesy-violation toward a parent that would otherwise require explanation. Second, and editorially more important, it produces ritual-impurity-by-association: the camel-saddle on which she sits, and the teraphim hidden within it, become untouchable for Lavan under the menstrual-impurity laws subsequently codified at Lev 15:19-24 (the *niddah* who sits on something makes it unclean; anyone who touches what she sits on is unclean until evening). The tacit invocation of menstrual-impurity defeats Lavan's search not by hiding the teraphim spatially but by making their position legally-and-ritually inaccessible.

**The chapter's deepest narrative-irony.** Rachel uses a ritual-purity claim — a claim invoking the laws that will later prohibit precisely the cult-objects she is hiding — to conceal her father's cult-objects. The structural irony is unmissable: the ritual-impurity framework (associated with the Leviticus-Deuteronomy-priestly stratum that polemicizes against teraphim — 1 Sam 15:23, 2 Kgs 23:24) is deployed to protect a teraphim from discovery. The two register-clashes — patriarchal household-cult vs. priestly purity-system; pre-monotheistic family-religion vs. centralized-cult prohibitionism — meet in a single concealment-act.

Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 220; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 496-497; Hamilton *NICOT* 1995 pp. 309-310; Wenham *WBC* 1994 p. 277. For the *niddah* legislation: Milgrom *Leviticus 1-16* AB 1991 on Lev 15.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּ֥חַר לְיַעֲקֹ֖ב וַיָּ֣רֶב בְּלָבָ֑ן וַיַּ֤עַן יַעֲקֹב֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְלָבָ֔ן מַה־פִּשְׁעִי֙ מַ֣ה חַטָּאתִ֔י כִּ֥י דָלַ֖קְתָּ אַחֲרָֽי׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov was angry, and contended with Lavan. And Ya'aqov answered and said to Lavan, What is my trespass? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued after me?

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־מִשַּׁ֣שְׁתָּ אֶת־כָּל־כֵּלַ֗י מַה־מָּצָ֙אתָ֙ מִכֹּ֣ל כְּלֵי־בֵיתֶ֔ךָ שִׂ֣ים כֹּ֔ה נֶ֥גֶד אַחַ֖י וְאַחֶ֑יךָ וְיוֹכִ֖יחוּ בֵּ֥ין שְׁנֵֽינוּ׃

i18n.en: Whereas you have felt about all my goods, what have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may judge between us two.

paragraphs.text: זֶה֩ עֶשְׂרִ֨ים שָׁנָ֤ה אָנֹכִי֙ עִמָּ֔ךְ רְחֵלֶ֥יךָ וְעִזֶּ֖יךָ לֹ֣א שִׁכֵּ֑לוּ וְאֵילֵ֥י צֹאנְךָ֖ לֹ֥א אָכָֽלְתִּי׃

i18n.en: These twenty years have I been with you; your ewes and your she-goats have not cast their young, and the rams of your flock I have not eaten.

paragraphs.text: טְרֵפָה֙ לֹא־הֵבֵ֣אתִי אֵלֶ֔יךָ אָנֹכִ֣י אֲחַטֶּ֔נָּה מִיָּדִ֖י תְּבַקְשֶׁ֑נָּה גְּנֻֽבְתִ֣י י֔וֹם וּגְנֻֽבְתִ֖י לָֽיְלָה׃

i18n.en: That which was torn of beasts I did not bring to you; I bore the loss of it; of my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night.

paragraphs.text: הָיִ֧יתִי בַיּ֛וֹם אֲכָלַ֥נִי חֹ֖רֶב וְקֶ֣רַח בַּלָּ֑יְלָה וַתִּדַּ֥ד שְׁנָתִ֖י מֵֽעֵינָֽי׃

i18n.en: Thus I was: in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from my eyes.

paragraphs.text: זֶה־לִּ֞י עֶשְׂרִ֣ים שָׁנָה֮ בְּבֵיתֶךָ֒ עֲבַדְתִּ֜יךָ אַרְבַּֽע־עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה שָׁנָה֙ בִּשְׁתֵּ֣י בְנֹתֶ֔יךָ וְשֵׁ֥שׁ שָׁנִ֖ים בְּצֹאנֶ֑ךָ וַתַּחֲלֵ֥ף אֶת־מַשְׂכֻּרְתִּ֖י עֲשֶׂ֥רֶת מֹנִֽים׃

i18n.en: These twenty years have I been in your house: I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock; and you have changed my wages ten times.

paragraphs.text: לוּלֵ֡י אֱלֹהֵ֣י אָבִי֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י אַבְרָהָ֜ם וּפַ֤חַד יִצְחָק֙ הָ֣יָה לִ֔י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה רֵיקָ֣ם שִׁלַּחְתָּ֑נִי אֶת־עָנְיִ֞י וְאֶת־יְגִ֧יעַ כַּפַּ֛י רָאָ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים וַיּ֥וֹכַח אָֽמֶשׁ׃

i18n.en: Except the Elohim of my father, the Elohim of Avraham, and the Fear of Yitzchaq, had been with me, surely now you had sent me away empty. Elohim has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands, and rebuked you last night.

notes.official:
***Pachad Yitzchaq* — *the Fear of Yitzchaq* — is a hapax-construction divine epithet** unique to Gen 31:42 and its recurrence at v 53 within Genesis. The construct *pachad* (*fear, dread, terror*) + *Yitzchaq* (the patriarchal personal name) is morphologically unparalleled in the wider patriarchal divine-name vocabulary, and has occupied two generations of critical scholarship.

**Two principal readings.** *(a) The traditional reading*: *pachad* takes its standard lexical sense (*fear, dread*), and the construct is an *objective-genitive divine epithet* — *the (deity who is) the object of Yitzchaq's fear* / *the One whom Yitzchaq feared*. The reading parallels the *Avir Ya'aqov* (*Mighty One of Ya'aqov*, Gen 49:24) and the *Elohei Avraham* (*Elohim of Avraham*) of the ancestral-god formula. The translation here is the ASV-baseline *the Fear of Yitzchaq*; the reading is preserved by **Alt** *Der Gott der Väter* 1929 (the foundational ancestral-god monograph), **Westermann** *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 498, and **Speiser** AB *Genesis* 1964.

*(b) The kinship reading*: **Albright** *JBL* 54 (1935) proposed that *pachad* is cognate with the Arabic *fakhdh* (*thigh, clan, kinsmen*) and the Aramaic *pakhda*; the construct then means *the Kinsman of Yitzchaq* — a divine-kinship-epithet paralleling the *Avir Ya'aqov* (read as *the Bull of Ya'aqov*, a clan-totem) and the *go'el* (kinsman-redeemer) terminology elsewhere. **Cross** *Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic* 1973 ch. 1 adopts the Albright reading as part of the broader patriarchal-El-religion reconstruction. **Malul** *VT* 35 (1985) defends. **Hillers** *JBL* 91 (1972) and *JBL* 92 (1973) disputes the etymological basis (the *fakhdh*-cognate is contested) and argues for retaining the traditional *fear* sense.

**The wider critical reception is genuinely divided** and has not converged. The ASV-baseline *Fear* is preserved here because (i) it is the standard English rendering; (ii) the *pachad*-as-fear sense is grammatically uncontested at every other *pachad* occurrence in the HB; (iii) the kinship reading is etymologically contested. The kinship-reading is documented in the [pachad-yitzchaq-fear-of-isaac-divine-epithet](#pachad-yitzchaq-fear-of-isaac-divine-epithet) glossary entry and is preserved as a defensible alternative.

**The construction belongs to the patriarchal ancestral-god religion** — each patriarchal lineage having its own ancestral-deity, with the deities sometimes preserved under epithets that name the patriarch by personal name. The pattern recurs at the *Avir Ya'aqov* (Gen 49:24); the *Elohei Avraham* / *Elohei Yitzchaq* / *Elohei Ya'aqov* formula; and (more sparsely) the *El Elohei Yisra'el* of Gen 33:20. The Gen 31:42 occurrence is the *Pachad Yitzchaq*'s first attestation; v 53 is the second-and-final HB occurrence.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֨עַן לָבָ֜ן וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶֽל־יַעֲקֹ֗ב הַבָּנ֨וֹת בְּנֹתַ֜י וְהַבָּנִ֤ים בָּנַי֙ וְהַצֹּ֣אן צֹאנִ֔י וְכֹ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֥ה רֹאֶ֖ה לִי־ה֑וּא וְלִבְנֹתַ֞י מָֽה־אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֤ה לָאֵ֙לֶּה֙ הַיּ֔וֹם א֥וֹ לִבְנֵיהֶ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָלָֽדוּ׃

i18n.en: And Lavan answered and said to Ya'aqov, The daughters are my daughters, and the children are my children, and the flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine; and what can I do this day for these my daughters, or for their children whom they have borne?

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּ֗ה לְכָ֛ה נִכְרְתָ֥ה בְרִ֖ית אֲנִ֣י וָאָ֑תָּה וְהָיָ֥ה לְעֵ֖ד בֵּינִ֥י וּבֵינֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And now, come, let us make a covenant, you and I; and let it be a witness between me and you.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֥ח יַעֲקֹ֖ב אָ֑בֶן וַיְרִימֶ֖הָ מַצֵּבָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov took a stone, and set it up as a pillar.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֤ב לְאֶחָיו֙ לִקְט֣וּ אֲבָנִ֔ים וַיִּקְח֥וּ אֲבָנִ֖ים וַיַּֽעֲשׂוּ־גָ֑ל וַיֹּ֥אכְלוּ שָׁ֖ם עַל־הַגָּֽל׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov said to his kinsmen, Gather stones. And they took stones, and made a heap; and they ate there by the heap.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָא־ל֣וֹ לָבָ֔ן יְגַ֖ר שָׂהֲדוּתָ֑א וְיַֽעֲקֹ֔ב קָ֥רָא ל֖וֹ גַּלְעֵֽד׃

i18n.en: And Lavan called it Yegar-Sahaduta, but Ya'aqov called it Gal-Ed.

notes.official:
**The verse stages the only continuous Aramaic phrase in Genesis.** *Yegar Sahaduta* (יְגַר שָׂהֲדוּתָא) is Imperial-Aramaic: *yegar* (*heap*, cognate with Hebrew *gal*) + *sahaduta* (*witness*, cognate with the late-biblical Hebrew *sahed* / *eduta* and the standard Aramaic *sahid*). Ya'aqov's Hebrew name *Gal-Ed* (גַּלְעֵד) — *heap of witness* — is the morpheme-for-morpheme Hebrew translation of the Aramaic. Both names mean the same thing; the narrator preserves both.

**The bilingual witness-heap stages the Lavan-Ya'aqov treaty across a language boundary.** Lavan the Arami (so designated repeatedly across the chapter — vv 20, 24) names the cairn in his Aramaic; Ya'aqov names it in his Hebrew. The narrator's preservation of both is a deliberate ethno-linguistic-pivot, marking the patriarch's separation from his Aramean kindred at the linguistic frontier as well as the geographical (the *nahar* of v 21 — the Euphrates). The two languages have functionally identical lexemes for the same concept, and the contrast is not communicative but identificatory: the names mark *who is speaking* rather than *what is being said*.

**The authenticity question.** Scholarly opinion is divided on whether the Aramaic phrase is (a) a genuine archaism preserving authentic Aramean-Hebrew bilingualism in the patriarchal-period stratum, or (b) a late editorial insertion projecting the Persian-period bilingual milieu back into the patriarchal narrative. Speiser AB *Genesis* 1964 pp. 247-248 reads the Aramaic as preserving authentic ethnic-linguistic context. Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 498-499 reads it as plausibly archaic and notes its hapax-status in the Pentateuch. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 221-222 preserves the question agnostic. The phrase's editorial significance does not depend on the authenticity-resolution: in either case, the narrator deploys the bilingual contrast as a marker of ethno-cultural separation at the moment of treaty.

The translation preserves both names in transliteration (*Yegar-Sahaduta* / *Gal-Ed*); the etymologies are made explicit in v 48 (*ha-gal ha-zeh ed* — *this heap is a witness*).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָבָ֔ן הַגַּ֨ל הַזֶּ֥ה עֵ֛ד בֵּינִ֥י וּבֵינְךָ֖ הַיּ֑וֹם עַל־כֵּ֥ן קָרָֽא־שְׁמ֖וֹ גַּלְעֵֽד׃

i18n.en: And Lavan said, This heap is a witness between me and you this day. Therefore was its name called Gal-Ed,

paragraphs.text: וְהַמִּצְפָּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָמַ֔ר יִ֥צֶף יְהוָ֖ה בֵּינִ֣י וּבֵינֶ֑ךָ כִּ֥י נִסָּתֵ֖ר אִ֥ישׁ מֵרֵעֵֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: and Mitzpah, for he said, YHWH watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another.

notes.official:
***V-ha-Mitzpah asher amar yitzef YHWH beini u-veinekha ki nisater ish me-re'ehu*** — *and Mitzpah, for he said, YHWH watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another*. The verse is the in-text etymology for the place-name *Mitzpah* (מִצְפָּה) on the root *tz-p-h* (*watch, look out, survey*); the verbal *yitzef* (jussive — *may he watch*) and the noun *mitzpah* (*watchpost*) share the root, producing the punning etymology *Mitzpah* = *the watchpost where YHWH watches*.

**The verse is the source of the modern Christian benediction known as the *Mizpah blessing*** (*The LORD watch between me and thee, while we are absent one from another*) — used in 19th- and 20th-century Anglo-American churches at parting ceremonies, on funeral cards, and in jewelry (the *Mizpah ring* and *Mizpah coin* traditions). The benediction-reception inverts the verse's original force. In context the *yitzef YHWH* clause is **not** a friendly farewell-blessing but a mutual-surveillance treaty-formula: Lavan and Ya'aqov, having just nearly come to blows, are invoking YHWH as a witness against future treaty-breach — *YHWH watch us, because we cannot watch each other when we are out of sight*. The continuation at vv 50-52 confirms the surveillance-register: Lavan threatens consequences if Ya'aqov afflicts his daughters or takes additional wives; v 52 prohibits each party from crossing the cairn-and-pillar boundary against the other *l-ra'ah* (*for harm*). The benediction-reception's affectionate sense is the opposite of the original mutual-distrust covenant.

**Cross-corpus place-name distribution.** The Gen 31:49 *Mitzpah* is the eponymous Gil'ad-frontier site (later: Judg 10:17, 11:11). Multiple *Mitzpah* / *Mitzpot* recur across the canon: Mitzpah of Binyamin (Josh 18:26; Judg 20:1; 1 Sam 7:5-16; Jer 40-41); Mitzpah of Yehudah (Josh 15:38); Mitzpah of Moav (1 Sam 22:3); Mitzpeh-Yisra'el (Josh 11:3). The toponym's reach reflects the watchtower function — many border-frontier sites carried the name. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 222; Westermann pp. 499-500.

paragraphs.text: אִם־תְּעַנֶּ֣ה אֶת־בְּנֹתַ֗י וְאִם־תִּקַּ֤ח נָשִׁים֙ עַל־בְּנֹתַ֔י אֵ֥ין אִ֖ישׁ עִמָּ֑נוּ רְאֵ֕ה אֱלֹהִ֥ים עֵ֖ד בֵּינִ֥י וּבֵינֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: If you afflict my daughters, and if you take wives besides my daughters, no man is with us; see, Elohim is witness between me and you.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לָבָ֖ן לְיַעֲקֹ֑ב הִנֵּ֣ה ׀ הַגַּ֣ל הַזֶּ֗ה וְהִנֵּה֙ הַמַצֵּבָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָרִ֖יתִי בֵּינִ֥י וּבֵינֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And Lavan said to Ya'aqov, Behold this heap, and behold the pillar, which I have set between me and you.

paragraphs.text: עֵ֚ד הַגַּ֣ל הַזֶּ֔ה וְעֵדָ֖ה הַמַּצֵּבָ֑ה אִם־אָ֗נִי לֹֽא־אֶֽעֱבֹ֤ר אֵלֶ֙יךָ֙ אֶת־הַגַּ֣ל הַזֶּ֔ה וְאִם־אַ֠תָּה לֹא־תַעֲבֹ֨ר אֵלַ֜י אֶת־הַגַּ֥ל הַזֶּ֛ה וְאֶת־הַמַּצֵּבָ֥ה הַזֹּ֖את לְרָעָֽה׃

i18n.en: This heap is witness, and the pillar is witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you, and that you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, for harm.

paragraphs.text: אֱלֹהֵ֨י אַבְרָהָ֜ם וֵֽאלֹהֵ֤י נָחוֹר֙ יִשְׁפְּט֣וּ בֵינֵ֔ינוּ אֱלֹהֵ֖י אֲבִיהֶ֑ם וַיִּשָּׁבַ֣ע יַעֲקֹ֔ב בְּפַ֖חַד אָבִ֥יו יִצְחָֽק׃

i18n.en: The Elohim of Avraham, and the Elohim of Nachor, the Elohim of their father, judge between us. And Ya'aqov swore by the Fear of his father Yitzchaq.

notes.official:
**The verse is structurally pivotal for three reasons.** *(i) The collateral-ancestral deployment of the *Elohei X v-Elohei Y* formula.* Lavan invokes both Avraham's deity *and* Nachor's deity, possibly as distinct ancestral-deities. The Alt 1929 *ancestral-god-religion* reconstruction reads this as the strongest patriarchal-cycle evidence for the clan-based ancestral-deity model: each patriarchal lineage has its own ancestral-deity, and the two deities are appositionally-distinguished here. Avraham and Nachor are brothers (Gen 11:26-29; 22:20-23 — the genealogical link) and would share a paternal lineage (Terach), but the formula treats their deities as distinct.

*(ii) The harmonizing apposition *Elohei avihem* (*the Elohim of their father*).* The closing clause — singular *avihem* — has been read as a Masoretic editorial harmonization that smooths the collateral-deity reading toward a single-Terach-ancestor identification (Sarna *JPS* 1989 p. 220; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 pp. 497-498). The Samaritan Pentateuch and some LXX witnesses omit the *Elohei avihem* clause, which is consistent with the harmonization-hypothesis: the apposition was added to assimilate the two collateral deities to a single Terach-deity.

*(iii) The *Pachad Yitzchaq* recurrence.* Ya'aqov's oath-formula deploys *Pachad aviv Yitzchaq* — *the Fear of his father Yitzchaq* — recurring the v 42 hapax divine-epithet and expanding it with *aviv*. This is the second-and-final HB occurrence of the *Pachad Yitzchaq* construction; see [pachad-yitzchaq-fear-of-isaac-divine-epithet](#pachad-yitzchaq-fear-of-isaac-divine-epithet) for the full philological discussion. The recurrence reinforces the v 42 occurrence and stages a structural-balance: Lavan swears by his ancestral-deities (Avraham and Nachor); Ya'aqov swears by his ancestral-deity (the Pachad of his father). Each party invokes his own clan-deity, and the cairn-and-pillar between them is the witness.

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov offered a sacrifice on the mountain, and called his kinsmen to eat bread. And they ate bread, and lodged on the mountain.
